topics.title: Threads, Data Races & Memory Safety
topics.description: Understanding multi-threaded execution, data races, race conditions, and memory visibility in modern C++.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A Data Race occurs when two concurrent threads access the same memory location simultaneously, at least one access is a write, and there is no synchronization. A data race is Undefined Behavior (UB) in C++.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Multi-core CPUs execute threads concurrently; unsynchronized writes cause corrupted state, silent calculation bugs, and memory crashes.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Coordinate access to shared mutable state using synchronization primitives (Mutex, Atomics, Lock Guards).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: std::jthread (C++20) provides RAII thread joining on scope exit.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Data Race = Undefined Behavior
callout.text: Two threads executing counter++ without synchronization causes lost increments and hardware cache inconsistency. In C++, data race is strict UB!

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: std::lock_guard guarantees mutual exclusion across 10 threads incrementing count.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Thread pools, concurrent order books, real-time gaming state sync.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use synchronization whenever mutable state is shared across threads.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not share mutable state if message passing (actor model) or thread-local storage suffices.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Thread-safe predictable execution.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Lock contention overhead.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: std::thread (C++11), std::jthread with auto-join (C++20).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to join or detach a std::thread before destruction, triggering std::terminate().

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between a Data Race and a Race Condition?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: A Data Race is unsynchronized concurrent memory access (strictly Undefined Behavior in C++). A Race Condition is a semantic timing flaw where output depends on non-deterministic thread execution order.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Build an accumulator summing numbers from 4 worker threads.

practice.title: Thread Safe Accumulator
practice.problemStatement: Build an accumulator summing numbers from 4 worker threads.

referenceCode.code: class Accumulator { double total{0}; mutex m; public: void add(double v) { lock_guard<mutex> l(m); total += v; } };

topics.title: std::mutex, std::lock_guard & std::unique_lock
topics.description: RAII-based mutual exclusion locking in C++.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: std::mutex provides mutual exclusion. std::lock_guard is an immovable RAII wrapper. std::unique_lock is a movable, flexible lock supporting manual unlock and condition variables.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Manually calling mtx.lock() and mtx.unlock() leaks locks when exceptions or early returns occur, causing permanent deadlocks.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Always wrap mutexes in RAII lock objects on the stack.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mtx); locks on creation and unlocks on destruction automatically.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: lock_guard vs unique_lock
callout.text: Default to std::lock_guard (or std::scoped_lock in C++17). Use std::unique_lock ONLY when you need deferred locking, manual unlocking, or std::condition_variable!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: std::lock_guard automatically releases vaultMutex even if an exception is thrown.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Banking ledgers, hardware controllers, memory allocators.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use lock_guard for standard critical sections. Use unique_lock with condition variables.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not hold locks during slow I/O or network requests.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Exception-safe locking; zero deadlock risk from forgotten unlocks.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Coarse locking reduces concurrency throughput.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: std::lock_guard, std::unique_lock, std::scoped_lock (C++17).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Calling mtx.lock() without RAII wrapper.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why is std::lock_guard preferred over manual mutex.lock()?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Because std::lock_guard is an RAII class that guarantees the mutex will be unlocked when exiting scope, even in the presence of early returns or thrown exceptions.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement transfer between two accounts using std::scoped_lock.

practice.title: Thread-Safe Bank Transfer
practice.problemStatement: Implement transfer between two accounts using std::scoped_lock.

referenceCode.code: void transfer(Account& from, Account& to, double amt) { std::scoped_lock lock(from.m, to.m); from.bal -= amt; to.bal += amt; }

topics.title: Read-Write Locks (std::shared_mutex)
topics.description: Optimizing read-heavy workloads with multiple concurrent readers and exclusive single writers.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: std::shared_mutex (C++17) allows multiple threads to acquire shared read access simultaneously (std::shared_lock) while granting exclusive access to a single writer (std::unique_lock).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: In read-heavy systems (e.g. 99% reads, 1% writes like DNS lookups or product catalog queries), standard mutexes serialize all readers, killing throughput.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Readers acquire std::shared_lock concurrently. Writers acquire std::unique_lock exclusively.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Multiple reader threads execute in parallel; writer thread blocks until all active readers finish.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: ThreadSafeCache enables concurrent read locks while guarding exclusive writes with unique_lock.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: DNS resolver cache, Stock symbol metadata lookup, Web server routing tables.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when read operations vastly outnumber write operations (>10:1 ratio).

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use if writes are frequent (shared_mutex has higher atomic overhead than standard mutex).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Massive throughput scaling for read-heavy workloads.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Risk of writer starvation if readers continuously hold shared locks.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: std::shared_mutex, std::shared_timed_mutex.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Acquiring unique_lock inside getter methods.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: When should you choose std::shared_mutex over std::mutex?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: When the workload is read-heavy (>90% reads). Multiple readers acquire shared_lock simultaneously without blocking each other.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement UserRegistry with concurrent get() and exclusive registerUser().

practice.title: Read-Heavy User Registry
practice.problemStatement: Implement UserRegistry with concurrent get() and exclusive registerUser().

referenceCode.code: class Registry { std::shared_mutex rw; public: void read() { std::shared_lock l(rw); } void write() { std::unique_lock l(rw); } };

topics.title: Deadlock Prevention & std::scoped_lock
topics.description: Preventing deadly mutual exclusion deadlocks using lock ordering, lock hierarchies, and std::scoped_lock.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A Deadlock occurs when two or more threads are permanently blocked, each holding a lock the other thread needs (Circular Wait: Thread 1 holds Mutex A and waits for B; Thread 2 holds Mutex B and waits for A).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Deadlocks freeze production systems, causing complete service outages requiring process restarts.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Coffman conditions: Eliminate Circular Wait by acquiring multiple mutexes in a globally consistent order.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: C++17 std::scoped_lock lock(mutexA, mutexB); uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm (via std::lock) to lock all mutexes safely.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: C++17 scoped_lock Deadlock Defense
callout.text: Always use std::scoped_lock lock(accountA.mtx, accountB.mtx); when acquiring multiple mutexes. It uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm automatically!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: std::scoped_lock locks both accounts atomically using deadlock-avoidance.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Bank account transfers, Dining Philosophers problem, Multi-resource transaction coordinators.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use std::scoped_lock whenever a function needs to lock 2 or more mutexes simultaneously.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not acquire locks in arbitrary order across different functions.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: 100% immune to circular wait deadlocks.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Slightly higher lock acquisition latency than single mutex.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Hierarchical Locking, Lock Ordering by pointer address, Deadlock Detection Graphs.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Acquiring Mutex A then Mutex B in Function 1, and Mutex B then Mutex A in Function 2.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What are the 4 Coffman conditions required for a deadlock to occur?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: 1. Mutual Exclusion, 2. Hold and Wait, 3. No Preemption, 4. Circular Wait. Breaking ANY ONE condition prevents deadlocks.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement pickForks() for philosopher using std::scoped_lock on left and right forks.

practice.title: Dining Philosophers Deadlock Fix
practice.problemStatement: Implement pickForks() for philosopher using std::scoped_lock on left and right forks.

referenceCode.code: void eat(Fork& left, Fork& right) { std::scoped_lock l(left.m, right.m); }

topics.title: Condition Variables & Producer-Consumer Queues
topics.description: Signaling and thread synchronization using std::condition_variable for blocking concurrent task queues.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: std::condition_variable is a synchronization primitive that allows threads to sleep (block) without consuming CPU cycles until notified by another thread that a condition is met.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Busy-waiting in a while(!ready) {} loop consumes 100% CPU on a core. Condition variables put threads to sleep efficiently.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Consumer calls cv.wait(lock, []{ return !queue.empty(); });. Producer pushes item and calls cv.notify_one().

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: cv.wait atomically unlocks the mutex and puts thread to sleep; when awakened, it reacquires the lock and checks predicate (defends against Spurious Wakeups).

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Spurious Wakeup Defense
callout.text: ALWAYS pass a predicate lambda to cv.wait(lock, [&]{ return !queue.empty(); }); to protect against spurious wakeups (waking up without a signal)!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: ThreadSafeQueue implements blocking pop() and notify_one() with condition variable.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Thread pool work-stealing queues, message brokers, logging background flushers.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use for producer-consumer pipelines, thread pools, and event dispatch queues.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not call cv.wait() without a predicate lambda (spurious wakeup bug).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Zero CPU usage while waiting; instant wakeup on data arrival.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires careful shutdown signaling.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: std::condition_variable (requires unique_lock), std::condition_variable_any.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Calling cv.wait without a lock or without a predicate loop.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is a Spurious Wakeup in multi-threading?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: A condition where a sleeping thread awakens from wait() even though no thread called notify(). Passing a predicate loop (cv.wait(lock, []{ return ready; })) ensures the thread re-checks the invariant before proceeding.

topics.title: std::atomic & Lock-Free Design Concepts
topics.description: Lock-free atomic primitives, memory orderings, and hardware CPU cache line synchronization in C++20.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: std::atomic<T> provides lock-free, race-free operations on primitive types using CPU hardware instructions (e.g. LOCK CMPXCHG on x86) without operating system mutex locks.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Mutex locks incur kernel context-switch overhead (microsecond scale). Atomics execute in hardware nanosecond cycles.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Hardware atomic instructions guarantee that read-modify-write operations (fetch_add, compare_exchange_strong) are indivisible.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Use std::atomic<int> for high-speed counters, sequence generators, and lock-free ring buffers.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: CAS (Compare-And-Swap)
callout.text: expected = 10; bool ok = atomicVal.compare_exchange_strong(expected, 20); // If atomicVal == 10, sets to 20 atomically. If not, updates expected with actual value!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: std::atomic handles 1,000,000 increments across 4 threads lock-free.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: High-frequency trading order matching, lock-free SPSC queues, real-time audio mixers.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use for simple counters, flags, and lock-free state machines.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not build complex lock-free data structures without expert knowledge of ABA problem and memory orderings.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Blazing fast performance; immune to deadlocks and priority inversion.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Difficult to write and debug complex lock-free data structures.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: std::atomic, std::atomic_flag, Memory orderings (relaxed, acquire, release, seq_cst).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Assuming non-primitive large structs are lock-free (check atomic.is_lock_free()).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the ABA problem in lock-free programming?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: A condition where Thread 1 reads value A, Thread 2 changes A -> B -> A, and Thread 1's Compare-And-Swap succeeds thinking the value never changed, causing memory corruption. Solved using tagged pointers or hazard pointers.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement a simple Spinlock using std::atomic_flag.

practice.title: Atomic Spinlock Mutex
practice.problemStatement: Implement a simple Spinlock using std::atomic_flag.

referenceCode.code: class Spinlock { std::atomic_flag flag = ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT; public: void lock() { while(flag.test_and_set(std::memory_order_acquire)) {} } void unlock() { flag.clear(std::memory_order_release); } };

sections.content: Mastering std::atomic & Lock-Free Design Concepts is essential for advanced C++ systems design.

topics.title: Thread-safe Singleton & Double-Checked Locking Trap
topics.description: Why naive double-checked locking was broken in C++98, and why Meyers Singleton is the optimal modern C++ solution.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A Thread-Safe Singleton guarantees exactly one instance is initialized safely under multi-threaded concurrency.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Naive singletons create race conditions where two threads simultaneously execute if (instance == nullptr) and instantiate two duplicate singletons.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: C++11 Meyers Singleton guarantees thread-safe initialization via static local variables.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: The compiler generates internal guards ensuring that only the first thread executes initialization while other threads wait.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: The Double-Checked Locking Anti-Pattern
callout.text: In C++98, DCLP (if (!inst) { lock; if (!inst) inst = new T(); }) was broken due to CPU out-of-order execution allocating memory before constructor finishes! In modern C++, always use Meyers Singleton!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Meyers Singleton executes constructor exactly once across 5 concurrent threads.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Logging engines, Configuration registries, Hardware drivers.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when an application strictly requires a single shared instance.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not write manual Double-Checked Locking with mutexes in modern C++.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Clean, zero manual locks, compiler-enforced thread safety.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Global state makes unit testing with mocks difficult.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Meyers Singleton, std::call_once with std::once_flag.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Implementing raw pointer DCLP without atomic acquire/release fences.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why was Double-Checked Locking broken before C++11?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Because CPU instruction reordering could reorder pointer assignment before the object constructor finished executing, allowing another thread to observe a non-null pointer to an uninitialized object.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement a thread-safe singleton using std::call_once and std::once_flag.

practice.title: std::call_once Singleton
practice.problemStatement: Implement a thread-safe singleton using std::call_once and std::once_flag.

referenceCode.code: class S { static void init() {} public: static void get() { static std::once_flag f; std::call_once(f, init); } };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Thread-safe Singleton & Double-Checked Locking Trap is essential for advanced C++ systems design.
